method: Opened History Today review (Campbell about 19,000; method; Pankhurst would reduce to about 10,000), Hurst book page (19,000; 19–20 percent of the capital’s population) and Gelaye 2025 (nearly 20,000 to 30,000). (sourcing pass)
text: After a grenade attack on Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani by two young Eritreans, Italian soldiers, Fascist Blackshirt militia and Italian civilians kill residents across Addis Ababa for three days. Ian Campbell (2017), checking Ethiopian testimony against foreign diplomats’ reports, estimates about 19,000 dead, close to a fifth of the city; historian Richard Pankhurst thought it nearer 10,000, and some writers give up to 30,000. In May 1937 Italian forces also shot the monks of the Debre Libanos monastery.
problem: Sources upgraded and estimates attributed by name; unsupported low figure dropped.

method: Opened Askew 2004 (survey of Japanese schools of estimates and why they differ) and the MOFA Q&A page; Britannica kept from the existing record. (sourcing pass)
text: After capturing Nanjing on 13 December 1937, Japanese troops kill prisoners of war and civilians on a mass scale, with widespread sexual violence, looting and arson; Japan’s Foreign Ministry says the killing of civilians cannot be denied. Estimates depend on the area, period and victims counted: China’s official figure is 300,000, the postwar Tokyo tribunal found more than 100,000 (in its verdict on General Matsui), Kasahara Tokushi estimates over 100,000 and perhaps nearly 200,000, and the more cautious Hata Ikuhiko about 38,000–42,000. Foreign residents led by John Rabe ran a Safety Zone that sheltered over 200,000 civilians.

method: Opened MERIP interview (100,000–110,000 moved; ‘two-thirds of them perished’; oral history method; restricted archives) and the Lamma review (16 camps). (sourcing pass)
text: To crush armed resistance in Cyrenaica (eastern Libya) led by Omar al-Mukhtar, Italian forces drive 100,000–110,000 people, mostly civilians, with their herds into 16 desert concentration camps; the regime called it “pacification”. Historian Ali Abdullatif Ahmida, who interviewed survivors for a decade, says about two-thirds of them died; Italian historian Emilio Gentile counts about 50,000 deaths, and exact totals are uncertain because Italian records are incomplete. Ahmida argues it was genocide; other historians call it an extreme colonial counter-insurgency.
